formation.title: Restoration of Nanzhao
formation.text:
The scattered peoples of Yunnan are united once more under a single banner. From the shores of Lake Erhai to the passes of the Ailao Mountains, the kingdom that once defied the Tang Dynasty and conquered the cities of the Irrawaddy is reborn.

But the character of this restoration remains to be determined. The Black Mywa warrior aristocracy stands ready to forge the kingdom through conquest, as their ancestors did when the Luojuzi, the Tiger Sons, led Nanzhao's armies to victories that shook the greatest empire on earth. Yet others point to Yunnan's position at the crossroads of civilizations, where the Southern Silk Road and the Tea Horse Road converge, and argue that commerce and culture will build a more enduring legacy than any sword.

What spirit shall define the reborn kingdom?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Raise the Tiger Banner. Let the Black Mywa ride to war!

modifiers.name: Tiger Banner of the Black Mywa
modifiers.text: The Black Mywa warrior caste, from which Nanzhao's rulers sprang, has reasserted its martial dominion. The Luojuzi, Tiger Sons, march again at the vanguard, their red helmets blazing like fire across the highlands. Every hundred men yields one Tiger Son, and every Tiger Son is worth ten ordinary soldiers.

options.text: Open the mountain passes. Let the caravans bring prosperity!

modifiers.name: Southern Silk Road
modifiers.text: Nanzhao straddles the crossroads of empires. The Tea Horse Road carries Pu'er tea to Tibet and brings back horses; the Southern Silk Road connects Burma, India, and China through Yunnan's mountain passes. Bai merchants and artisans transform this geographic blessing into lasting prosperity.

advances.name: Luojuzi Tradition
advances.text: The Luojuzi, Tiger Sons, were Nanzhao's elite vanguard. For every hundred soldiers, the strongest was chosen. They wore red helmets, leather armor, and bronze shields, yet fought barefoot for speed and agility.

advances.name: Yunnan Salt Extraction
advances.text: Salt wells dotted the Yunnan landscape, providing a crucial revenue source controlled by the crown. Salt and gold were mined in many parts of the kingdom.

advances.name: Mywa Caste System
advances.text: Nanzhao society divided into the administrative White Mywa of western Yunnan and the militaristic Black Mywa of the east. This dual-caste system provided both governance and martial prowess.

advances.name: Legacy of the Six Zhaos
advances.text: In 738, Piluoge united the Six Zhaos, the six principalities of western Yunnan, into a single kingdom under Tang recognition. This unification created the foundation for Nanzhao's power.

advances.name: Azhali Buddhism
advances.text: The esoteric Tantric school known as Azhali Buddhism was unique to Yunnan, blending Indian Vajrayana traditions with local spiritual practices and devotion to Avalokitesvara.

advances.name: Highland Warfare
advances.text: Nanzhao warriors exploited the rugged terrain of Yunnan (mountain passes, jungle valleys, and river gorges) to defeat armies many times their size.

advances.name: Bai Weaving Tradition
advances.text: The Bai people developed distinctive tie-dye techniques for cotton and silk fabrics, creating patterns that became famous across the region.

advances.name: Elephant Warfare
advances.text: Nanzhao chieftains rode war elephants into battle. The kingdom's elephant-hide lacquered armor was prized throughout the region as nearly impervious to arrows.

advances.name: Zhunu Crossbow Guards
advances.text: The Red Crossbow, Zhunu, guard units wielded powerful mounted crossbows that could bring down cavalry at extreme range. During sieges, crossbow fire from the walls cut down hundreds of attackers.

advances.name: Tianbao War Legacy
advances.text: The decisive victory over the Tang invasion of 751 proved that Nanzhao could stand against the mightiest empire on earth. This legacy of defiance defined the kingdom's identity.

event.title: Legacy of the Tianbao War
event.text:
In 751, when the Tang governor of Jiannan marched 80,000 soldiers into Yunnan to punish what he saw as a rebellious vassal, King Geluofeng met the invasion at Xiaguan. The battle was decisive: the Tang army was annihilated, their governor slain, and their ambitions to subjugate Nanzhao shattered for a generation.

The victory echoed across Asia. It proved that a highland kingdom of skilled warriors, fighting on familiar terrain, could humble even the mightiest empire. The Tianbao War became the founding myth of Nanzhao's independence: the moment when a confederation of mountain tribes proved itself a sovereign power.

How shall we honor this legacy?

options.text: The Tiger Sons shall always lead from the front.

modifiers.name: Tiger Sons Resurgent
modifiers.text: The spirit of the Tianbao War victory burns in Nanzhao's armies. The Tiger Sons lead from the front, and lesser men find courage in their example.

options.text: Strength earns respect, and respect brings peace.

modifiers.name: Diplomatic Equilibrium
modifiers.text: Having proven that even the Tang cannot overwhelm the kingdom by force, Nanzhao negotiates from a position of strength. The balance between great powers is Yunnan's shield.

advances.name: Three Pagodas of Chongsheng
advances.text: The Qianxun Pagoda and the Chongsheng Temple complex, with 890 rooms and 11,400 Buddha statues, represented the pinnacle of Nanzhao's spiritual and architectural achievement.

event.title: The Three Pagodas of Chongsheng
event.text:
King Quan Fengyou commissioned the greatest architectural achievement in Yunnan's history: the Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple. The central Qianxun Pagoda rises nearly seventy meters into the sky: one of the tallest structures in all of China. Together with the temple complex of 890 rooms and 11,400 Buddha statues, it stands as the spiritual heart of the kingdom.

Azhali Buddhism, the Tantric school unique to Yunnan, finds its grandest expression here. Worship of Avalokitesvara, the Great Black Deva, and the Guardian King of the North draws pilgrims from across the Buddhist world. The monastery's monks preserve learning, practice medicine, and advise the throne.

options.text: May the Three Pagodas stand for ten thousand years.

modifiers.name: Blessings of Chongsheng
modifiers.text: The Three Pagodas stand as eternal guardians of the faith and the realm. Pilgrims from across Asia journey to Chongsheng, and their devotion enriches both the spiritual and temporal power of the kingdom.

advances.name: Yunnan Copper Mining
advances.text: Yunnan held the largest copper reserves in China. The extraction and smelting of copper was a major industry, producing raw material for coins, weapons, and ceremonial objects.

advances.name: Imperial Court Culture
advances.text: When King Shilong proclaimed himself emperor and reoriented the kingdom around Buddhism, he established a court culture that blended Tang sophistication with Bai traditions.

advances.name: Conquest of the Pyu
advances.text: In the 830s, Nanzhao decimated the ancient Pyu city-states of the Irrawaddy valley, capturing artisans, scholars, and musicians who enriched the kingdom's culture.

event.title: Conquest of the Pyu City-States
event.text:
In the 830s, Nanzhao's armies swept down from the highlands into the Irrawaddy valley, where the ancient Pyu civilization had flourished for centuries. One by one, the great Pyu cities (Sri Ksetra, Halingyi, Binnaka) fell to the Tiger Banner. The Pyu kingdom, weakened by internal divisions, could not withstand the onslaught.

This was not mere raiding. Nanzhao carried off skilled artisans, musicians, and scholars, enriching its own culture with Pyu achievements. The conquest opened the road to Burma and the Indian Ocean, transforming Nanzhao from a highland power into a regional empire.

How shall we govern our new domains?

options.text: Plant the Tiger Banner on the banks of the Irrawaddy.

modifiers.name: Lords of the Irrawaddy
modifiers.text: The conquest of the Pyu demonstrated Nanzhao's ability to project power far beyond its highland heartland. The Irrawaddy valley falls under the shadow of the Tiger Banner.

options.text: Bind the Pyu as tributaries: their wealth serves us better than their ruin.

modifiers.name: Pyu Tributary Network
modifiers.text: Rather than rule by the sword alone, Nanzhao draws the conquered Pyu cities into a web of tributary relationships. Their wealth flows upstream, and their autonomy buys their loyalty.

advances.name: Meng Cavalry Tradition
advances.text: The Mengshe clan, from which Nanzhao's rulers descended, bred highland horses and trained cavalry skilled in mountain warfare and rapid flanking maneuvers.

advances.name: Tea Horse Road
advances.text: The ancient caravan route carrying Pu'er tea to Tibet and bringing back horses became one of Asia's great commercial arteries, with Yunnan as its indispensable hub.

event.title: Dominion of the Tea Horse Road
event.text:
The ancient caravan routes through Yunnan have grown into one of the great commercial arteries of Asia. The Tea Horse Road carries Pu'er tea northward to Tibet and Sichuan, where it is traded for horses, salt, and silver. The Southern Silk Road connects China to Burma, India, and beyond, with Yunnan as the indispensable waypoint.

Caravanserais dot the mountain passes. Bai merchants handle trade in a dozen languages. The toll revenues and transit taxes fill the royal treasury, and Yunnan's position as the middleman between civilizations makes it wealthier than its modest territory might suggest.

modifiers.name: Tea Horse Prosperity
modifiers.text: The Tea Horse Road is the lifeline of highland commerce. Yunnan tea for Tibetan horses, Chinese silk for Burmese gems: the caravans never rest, and the toll revenues never cease.

advances.name: Lacquered Armor Tradition
advances.text: Dali produced some of the finest lacquered leather armor in Asia, made from elephant hide and treated until it was almost as hard as iron. Sets were sent to the Song court as diplomatic gifts.

advances.name: Yunnan Silversmithing
advances.text: Yunnan's silver mines and its tradition of intricate filigree work produced jewelry and ceremonial objects prized across the region.

advances.name: Bai Literary Tradition
advances.text: Bai poetry and prose, influenced by the Chinese literary tradition but written in the Bai language, reached remarkable heights during the Dali period.

advances.name: Highland Fortification
advances.text: Nanzhao's mountain fortresses exploited the natural terrain (narrow passes, sheer cliffs, and river gorges) to create defensive positions that multiplied the defenders' advantage.

advances.name: Dali Marble Craft
advances.text: The distinctive marble quarried near Dali, with its unique natural patterns, was prized for construction and artistic purposes across southern China.

advances.name: Standing Army Reform
advances.text: At its height, Nanzhao maintained a standing army of 100,000 experienced troops under strict military law: a remarkable achievement for a highland kingdom.

advances.name: Salt Monopoly
advances.text: Crown control over Yunnan's salt wells provided a reliable revenue stream that funded both the court and the army.

advances.name: Multi-Ethnic Governance
advances.text: Yunnan's diverse population (Bai, Yi, Tai, Tibetan, and others) required flexible governance that accommodated different customs while maintaining central authority.

advances.name: Pu'er Tea Mastery
advances.text: Yunnan's Pu'er tea, aged and compressed into bricks for transport on the Tea Horse Road, became one of Asia's most valuable trade commodities.

advances.name: Avalokitesvara Devotion
advances.text: Devotion to Avalokitesvara (Guanyin, the Goddess of Mercy) was central to Azhali Buddhism. The state religion unified the diverse peoples of Yunnan under a shared spiritual identity, and gilt bronze images of the Acuoye Guanyin were cast for its altars.

advances.name: Mountain Pass Control
advances.text: Yunnan's mountain passes were natural chokepoints for both armies and trade. Controlling them meant controlling access to the entire southwestern frontier.

advances.name: Lacquer Guard Tradition
advances.text: Elite troops clad in the famous lacquered elephant-hide armor represented the pinnacle of Nanzhao's military craftsmanship, warriors as hardened as the armor they wore.

advances.name: Centralized Administration
advances.text: The crown consolidated control over Yunnan's diverse provinces, replacing the loose confederation of the early period with a more centralized bureaucratic apparatus.

advances.name: Yunnan Mining Boom
advances.text: Yunnan's vast silver and copper deposits fueled an economic boom. The province's silver production would eventually contribute millions of taels to China's national output.

advances.name: Tea Trade Expansion
advances.text: As demand for Yunnan's tea spread across Asia, the network of caravan routes expanded, connecting ever more distant markets to the Pu'er tea warehouses.

advances.name: Highland Defense Doctrine
advances.text: Centuries of highland warfare crystallized into a formal doctrine: use the terrain, harass supply lines, avoid pitched battles on open ground, and let the mountains fight for you.

advances.name: Bai Artistic Renaissance
advances.text: Under centralized patronage, Bai artists achieved new heights in painting, sculpture, metalwork, and architecture, synthesizing influences from China, Tibet, and Southeast Asia.

advances.name: Modern Governance
advances.text: The traditional institutions of Yunnan are reformed to meet the challenges of a changing world, balancing the heritage of the Mywa caste system with modern administrative efficiency.

advances.name: Industrial Mining
advances.text: Modern techniques transform Yunnan's ancient mining industry, vastly increasing the output of copper, silver, tin, and lead.

advances.name: Bai Scholarship
advances.text: A new generation of Bai scholars combines the literary traditions of their ancestors with modern methods of inquiry, producing works of lasting significance.

advances.name: Commercial Modernization
advances.text: The ancient caravan routes are modernized with better roads, standardized weights and measures, and formal commercial treaties.

advances.name: Modern Military
advances.text: Highland defense traditions are supplemented with modern drill, organization, and tactics, creating an army that combines mountain expertise with contemporary discipline.

advances.name: Nanzhao National Identity
advances.text: The diverse peoples of Yunnan forge a shared national consciousness, drawing on the legacy of the six united zhaos, the Three Pagodas, and the Tea Horse Road.

destiny.name: Destiny of Nanzhao
destiny.text: The kingdom is reborn, but its destiny is yet unwritten. Stabilize the realm and choose the path that will define Nanzhao for generations.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of Nanzhao
event.text: The kingdom stands restored, its people united under the old banner. The foundation is laid, now the question is what we shall build upon it. The Black Mywa warriors sharpen their blades while the Bai merchants count their silver. Both paths lead to glory, but of very different kinds.

destiny.name: Conquest of the Shan States
destiny.text: The Shan highlands east of Yunnan are fragmented among petty rulers. To extend the Tiger Banner's reach, bring Kengtung and Hsenwi under Nanzhao's dominion and raise an army worthy of the Black Mywa.

conditions.text: Chose Tiger Banner of the Black Mywa
Own Kengtung, or a subject owns it
Own Hsenwi, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 30

event.title: The Shan States Submit
event.text:
The fragmented Shan principalities have been brought to heel. From Kengtung's valleys to Hsenwi's highlands, the Tiger Banner now flies where once a dozen petty lords squabbled over scraps. The Shan chiefs kneel before the throne of Nanzhao, and their warriors swell our ranks.

This is only the beginning. The Irrawaddy valley beckons to the south: the ancient road to empire that our ancestors walked when they destroyed the Pyu and shook the foundations of the world.

options.text: The Shan bow to the Tiger Banner.

destiny.name: Empire of the Irrawaddy
destiny.text: The ancient Pyu cities of the Irrawaddy valley once fell to Nanzhao's armies. Repeat that feat by conquering Pagan and Thaton and holding half of the Irrawaddy valley, building an empire that stretches from Yunnan's highlands to the sea.

conditions.text: Own Pagan, or a subject owns it
Own Thaton, or a subject owns it
Army size at least 50
We or our non-sovereign subjects hold at least 50% of the locations in the Irrawady area

event.title: The Tiger Banner Over Burma
event.text:
Pagan has fallen. Thaton has fallen. The great cities of the Irrawaddy valley, which once belonged to the Pyu before our ancestors razed them, are ours again. The ghost of King Quan Fengyou smiles from the heavens as the Tiger Banner is planted on the banks of the river that feeds Burma.

An empire now stretches from the highlands of Yunnan to the lowlands of the Irrawaddy delta. But empires must be governed as well as conquered. How shall we consolidate these vast new territories?

options.text: Press forward: the Tiger Sons halt for nothing.

modifiers.name: Tiger March
modifiers.text: The Tiger Sons lead the army forward without pause. Enemies submit or are swept aside. The pace of conquest strains the treasury and the people, but the Black Mywa know no other way.

options.text: Fortify what we hold and build strength.

modifiers.name: Highland Consolidation
modifiers.text: The empire pauses to digest its conquests. Reinforcements flow in, garrisons are established, and mercenaries supplement the army while the highland core recovers.

destiny.name: The Tiger Empire
destiny.text: The ultimate vision of the Black Mywa: an empire that dominates both the fertile Sichuan basin and the Irrawaddy lowlands. Take Chengdu and Sagaing to command the two great river systems of the mainland.

conditions.text: Own Chéngdū, or a subject owns it
Own Sagaing, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Army size at least 75

event.title: The Tiger Empire
event.text:
Chengdu and Sagaing stand under the Tiger Banner. The fertile Sichuan basin, breadbasket of China, feeds our coffers, while the Irrawaddy lowlands secure our dominion over mainland Southeast Asia. No highland kingdom in history has achieved what Nanzhao has built: an empire spanning the two great river systems of the Asian mainland.

The Black Mywa dreamed of this for generations. Now we must decide the character of the empire we have forged. Shall the sword remain our instrument, or shall the institutions of governance temper the blade?

options.text: The sword built this empire: the sword shall sustain it.

modifiers.name: Sword Emperor
modifiers.text: The emperor rules by the sword and through the warrior nobility. Noble levies swell the army, and new weapons of war thunder across the battlefield, though the cost of endless expansion strains the treasury.

options.text: Empire requires governance, not just conquest.

modifiers.name: Highland Mandate
modifiers.text: The empire adopts the trappings of legitimate governance. The warrior king becomes an emperor with a mandate, recognized and feared by all the world's great powers.

destiny.name: Tea Horse Dominion
destiny.text: The Tea Horse Road connects Yunnan to Tibet, carrying Pu'er tea north and horses south. Extend Nanzhao's commercial reach to Lhasa itself and amass a treasury worthy of the Southern Silk Road.

conditions.text: Chose Southern Silk Road
Own Lhasa, or a subject owns it
Gold at least 1000
Stability at least 25

event.title: The Tea Horse Road Is Ours
event.text:
Lhasa, the rooftop of the world, now trades through our hands. The Tea Horse Road, that ancient artery carrying Pu'er tea to Tibet and returning horses and silver, belongs entirely to Nanzhao. From the tea gardens of Simao to the monasteries of central Tibet, every brick of compressed tea and every Tibetan pony passes through our territory.

The caravansaries are full, the toll houses overflow, and the Bai merchants smile as they count the profits of geography made manifest.

options.text: The caravans shall bring us the world's wealth.

destiny.name: Crossroads of Asia
destiny.text: Yunnan sits at the meeting point of Chinese, Indian, Tibetan, and Southeast Asian civilizations. Extend the trade network to Angkor, put our Bai merchants to work in four markets at once, and transform the kingdom into Asia's commercial crossroads.

conditions.text: Own Angkor, or a subject owns it
Num of markets with merchants at least 4
Gold at least 2000

event.title: Crossroads of Asia
event.text:
What began as a mountain kingdom's control of a few caravan routes has become something extraordinary. Nanzhao's trade network now stretches from the tea gardens of Yunnan to the temples of Angkor. Chinese silk, Tibetan silver, Burmese gems, and Khmer spices all pass through our markets.

Bai merchants handle commerce in a dozen languages. Our merchants keep their own houses in four markets, and traders across the continent settle their accounts in Dali. Yunnan has become what geography always intended: the crossroads of Asia.

options.text: Extend the network: more merchants, more routes.

modifiers.name: Merchant Network
modifiers.text: Bai merchants fan out across the continent, establishing trading posts and diplomatic connections. Every new route brings new partnerships, and Yunnan's influence spreads through silver rather than steel.

options.text: Invest in our artisans and integrate our peoples.

modifiers.name: Artisan Guilds
modifiers.text: The kingdom invests in its diverse population. Bai silversmiths, Yi weavers, Tai potters: all find a place in prosperous guilds that strengthen the social fabric while enriching the treasury.

destiny.name: Emporium of Asia
destiny.text: From Vientiane to Guangzhou, the Southern Silk Road links the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea. Control both endpoints, build up Tàihé, the capital on Lake Erhai, to 54 development, and build the greatest trading empire mainland Asia has ever seen.

conditions.text: Own Vientiane, or a subject owns it
Own Guǎngzhōu, or a subject owns it
We own Tàihé and its development is at least 54
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Emporium of Asia
event.text:
From Vientiane to Guangzhou, the Southern Silk Road is ours. The greatest commercial artery of mainland Asia, connecting the Indian Ocean trade to the South China Sea, runs through Nanzhao's territory. No merchant crosses our borders without leaving silver behind.

The Bai trading diaspora spans the continent. Our markets set prices that merchants in Canton and Calcutta must accept. The kingdom that began as six highland chieftains has become the commercial heart of Asia.

options.text: Let all nations come to trade in our markets.

modifiers.name: World Emporium
modifiers.text: The markets of Nanzhao welcome traders from every nation and faith. Buddhist monasteries bless the commerce, mercenary companies protect the roads, and the kingdom's explorers seek ever more distant partners.

options.text: The merchants shall share power with the throne.

modifiers.name: Merchant Kings
modifiers.text: The old warrior nobility yields to a new mercantile aristocracy. Burgher wealth and guild power reshape the kingdom's institutions, with the temple clergy mediating between crown and commerce.

units.name: Luojuzi
units.text: The Tiger Sons, Nanzhao's elite vanguard. One chosen from every hundred soldiers, they wear red helmets, leather armor, and bronze shields, fighting barefoot for speed.

units.name: Wuman Warriors
units.text: Clan fighters of the Black Mywa, the hill peoples east of Dali whom the Chinese called Wuman. They come down from their ridges in felt cloaks and lacquered leather under their own chiefs, strike from ambush with spear and crossbow, and go home when the chief who led them falls.

units.name: Nanzhao War Elephant
units.text: Chieftains rode armored elephants into battle, their lacquered elephant-hide barding deflecting arrows and spears. The psychological impact alone was devastating.

units.name: Zhunu Crossbow Guard
units.text: The Red Crossbow guards, armed with powerful mounted crossbows, excelled in both field battle and siege defense among the mountains of Yunnan.

units.name: Meng Cavalry
units.text: Highland horsemen of the Mengshe ruling clan, trained in mountain warfare. Swift flankers who exploit the terrain that cripples heavier cavalry.

units.name: Yunnan Garrison Infantry
units.text: Professional soldiers of Nanzhao's standing army, equipped and trained under strict military law. Hardy mountain fighters who hold their ground against any assault.

units.name: Dali Lacquer Guard
units.text: Elite infantry clad in the famous lacquered elephant-hide armor, almost as hard as iron, yet lighter and more flexible. The finest soldiers in Yunnan.

buildings.name: Salt Wells
buildings.text: Extraction facilities for Yunnan's abundant salt deposits, a crucial revenue source controlled by the crown since the days of the first Nanzhao kings.

where.text: Salt is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Chongsheng Monastery
buildings.text: A grand Buddhist temple complex modeled on the historical Chongsheng Temple with its Three Pagodas: the spiritual heart of the Nanzhao and Dali kingdoms.

buildings.name: Copper Smelter
buildings.text: Facilities for extracting and smelting the vast copper deposits of Yunnan: the largest reserves in China, feeding an insatiable demand for coinage and weaponry.

where.text: Copper is produced in the location's market

buildings.name: Caravanserai
buildings.text: Rest stops and trading posts along the Tea Horse Road and Southern Silk Road, where merchants from China, Tibet, Burma, and India exchange goods and information.

buildings.name: Lacquer Armory
buildings.text: Workshops producing the famous Dali lacquered armor from elephant hide: treated and hardened until almost as resistant as iron, yet lighter and more flexible.

buildings.name: Dragon Pass Fort
buildings.text: A wall and gate thrown across a mountain defile, after the Dragon Head and Dragon Tail passes that closed the Dali plain between the Cangshan range and Lake Erhai. An army that cannot force the gate must find another way over the mountain.

buildings.name: Pu'er Tea Warehouse
buildings.text: Storage facilities for aging and compressing Yunnan's prized Pu'er tea into bricks for transport along the Tea Horse Road.

buildings.name: Azhali Temple
buildings.text: A temple of the Tantric Azhali Buddhist school unique to Yunnan, devoted to Avalokitesvara and the Great Black Deva.

buildings.name: Silver Workshop
buildings.text: A Bai artisan workshop specializing in intricate silver filigree jewelry: a craft tradition that has made Dali famous across Yunnan and beyond.

buildings.name: Bai Tie-Dye Workshop
buildings.text: A workshop of the Bai towns around Lake Erhai, where plain cloth is bound, dyed in indigo, and sold as patterned cloth far beyond Yunnan. It is found where the Bai are the people of the place.

buildings.name: Cangshan Marble Quarry
buildings.text: A quarry in marble country, like those on the slopes of the Cangshan range above Dali. Its stone carries veins that read as mountains and clouds, and is sought for building and for the slabs set into screens and furniture. The quarry raises the marble the land yields.

where.text: The location's raw material is Marble

buildings.name: Tea Mountain Garden
buildings.text: A hillside of old tea trees in tea country, like the six tea mountains beyond the Lancang. The leaf is pressed into bricks and cakes on the spot and carried north with the caravans.

where.text: The location's raw material is Tea

buildings.name: Imperial War Camp
buildings.text: A fortified command post for coordinating campaigns across the vast Tiger Empire, combining highland fortress design with the logistics needed to project power from Yunnan to Sichuan and the Irrawaddy.

buildings.name: Crossroads Emporium
buildings.text: A grand trading hall where merchants from China, Tibet, Burma, India, and Southeast Asia converge to exchange goods under Nanzhao's protection and profit.

list.name: Qingping Council
list.text: The qingping guan (six chief ministers drawn from the leading clans of the Six Zhao confederation) formed the supreme advisory cabinet of Nanzhao kings, modeled on Tang chancellery practice but adapted to highland aristocratic realities. The council deliberated on warfare, taxation, and embassy, while jealously excluding merchants and outsiders from central decision-making. Its strength lay in legitimizing royal decrees through aristocratic consensus; its weakness, in slowing the spread of crown control into the lowlands and counting houses.

list.name: Acharya Master-State
list.text: The Azhali (阿吒力) tantric Buddhist masters served the Dali Kingdom of 937-1253 not only as ritual officiants but as scribes, archivists, and chancery clerks staffing the royal administration. Their authority flowed through master-disciple lineages rather than birth, breaking the monopoly of the old aristocratic clans on literate office. A maintained Acharya state spreads literacy and integrates conquered peoples through shared ritual; neglected, it merely entrenches a clergy that has displaced the nobles without governing in their stead.

conditions.text: Any of

list.name: Tusi Chieftaincy System
list.text: The tusi (土司) framework, formalized under the Yuan and intensified by the Ming, recognized hereditary native chieftains of the Yi, Bai, Hmong, and Tai peoples as the realm's local administrators in exchange for tribute and levies. The system raised formidable highland armies and pacified frontiers cheaply, but each generation of confirmed inheritance hardened the chieftains into a parallel power that the throne could not safely dismantle. Letting the system decay does not weaken the chieftains: it merely starves the central registers that once tracked them.

conditions.text: Total development at least 1000

list.name: Tea-Horse Office (Chamasi)
list.text: From late Tang into the Ming, the chamasi (茶馬司) was a state monopoly office regulating the cross-frontier tea-for-horses trade along the Tea Horse Road through Yunnan. Officials taxed caravans, fixed exchange ratios between brick tea and frontier mounts, and licensed approved merchant houses, capturing for the throne the wealth of one of medieval Asia's most lucrative trade circuits. A working chamasi turns the Southern Silk Road into a fiscal artery; a decayed one breeds smuggling networks, frontier raids on under-guarded caravans, and lost tolls.

conditions.text: Total development at least 800
